intro: Every month, on a set schedule, the government releases two numbers that move markets and make headlines: how fast prices are rising and how many people cannot find work. Every three months it releases a third, the total value of everything the country produced. Presidents quote them, and the Federal Reserve sets interest rates with them in mind. A worker in Peoria, a farmer near Champaign and a trader in Chicago all feel what these numbers measure, even if they never read the reports.

This unit teaches you to build those numbers yourself and to read them with care. You will add up a country's output with the formula C + I + G + NX and separate real growth from rising prices. You will build a price index from a market basket, compute inflation and real wages, and sort adults into the employed, the unemployed and those outside the labor force. Each chapter also asks what a number leaves out: unpaid work, pollution, discouraged workers, the family whose costs rise faster than the average.

By the end you will be able to take a headline such as GDP grew 3% or unemployment fell to 4% and explain how it was measured. You will check the arithmetic and say what the number does and does not tell you about how people are living. That is the foundation for the rest of macroeconomics, because the business cycle, fiscal policy and the Federal Reserve all start from these measurements.
bigQuestion: How do we measure how well a whole economy is doing, and what can those numbers hide?

timeline.t: Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations treats a nation's yearly produce as the measure of its wealth
The Bureau of Labor Statistics begins publishing cost-of-living indexes for cities, the roots of today's CPI
Unemployment reaches about 25% at the depth of the Great Depression
Simon Kuznets gives the U.S. Senate the first official estimates of national income
A monthly household survey of jobs begins; it grows into today's Current Population Survey
The Employment Act makes maximum employment a goal of the federal government
Congress directs the Federal Reserve to promote maximum employment and stable prices
Consumer price inflation reaches about 13.5% for the year
The Bureau of Economic Analysis switches its headline measure of output from GNP to GDP
Unemployment climbs to about 10% after the financial crisis
Unemployment jumps to 14.7% in April as the pandemic closes businesses
The 12-month inflation rate peaks near 9%, the highest in about four decades

words.d: the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a period, usually a year
a good or service sold to the person or business that will use it, not resell it or make it into something else
GDP measured in the prices of a fixed base year, so it changes only when actual output changes
GDP divided by population; output per person
the CPI; the Bureau of Labor Statistics' monthly measure of the prices city households pay for a market basket
a fixed list of goods and services in fixed amounts that stands for what a typical buyer purchases
the percent change in a price index over a period, usually a year
pay adjusted for inflation, which shows what the pay can actually buy
all people 16 and older who are employed or unemployed; everyone working or looking for work
the number unemployed divided by the labor force, times 100
the labor force divided by the adult population, times 100; the share of adults working or looking
the unemployment rate at full employment, made up of frictional and structural unemployment

test.q: A mill sells $300 of flour to a bakery, which sells $1,000 of bread to shoppers. The contribution to GDP is:
test.why: Only the final sale counts. The flour is an intermediate good already inside the $1,000 of bread.

test.q: C = $600 billion, I = $100 billion, G = $150 billion, X = $50 billion and M = $80 billion. GDP is:
Which of these is counted in this year's U.S. GDP?
choices: A share of stock bought for $2,000
A new combine built this year at a plant in Illinois
test.why: The combine is a new good produced inside the country. Stock is a financial trade, the check is a transfer and the couch is used.

test.q: Nominal GDP is $26 trillion and the GDP deflator is 130. Real GDP is:
test.why: Real GDP = nominal / deflator x 100 = 26 / 130 x 100 = 20 trillion.

test.q: Why is real GDP per capita a better rough measure of living standards than nominal GDP?
choices: It removes the effects of rising prices and a growing population
It includes unpaid work at home
It subtracts the cost of pollution
test.why: Real GDP holds prices fixed, and dividing by population gives output per person.

test.q: A parent quits a paid job to care for a child at home. Measured GDP:
choices: Rises, because child care is valuable
Falls, even though the care is still being given
Rises by the cost of day care
test.why: The lost wages leave GDP, and the unpaid care is not counted because no one pays for it.

test.q: A market basket costs $150 in the base year and $162 this year. The price index is:
test.why: Index = 162 / 150 x 100 = 108. Prices are 8% above the base year.

test.q: The CPI goes from 250 to 265. The inflation rate is:
test.why: (265 - 250) / 250 x 100 = 15 / 250 x 100 = 6%. Dividing by 265 instead gives the wrong 5.7%.

test.q: Your wage rises 2% while prices rise 5%. Your real wage:
test.why: Real wage growth is about nominal growth minus inflation: 2 - 5 = -3%.

test.q: Which group is usually hurt by unexpectedly high inflation?
choices: Savers and lenders who are repaid in fixed dollars
Workers whose pay rises with the CPI
test.why: Lenders and savers get back fixed dollars that now buy less. Borrowers gain, and CPI-linked pay keeps up.

test.q: A town has 18,000 people employed and 2,000 unemployed. The unemployment rate is:
test.why: Labor force = 20,000. Rate = 2,000 / 20,000 x 100 = 10%. Dividing by the employed gives the wrong 11.1%.

test.q: Which person is NOT in the labor force?
choices: A laid-off worker who is sending out applications
A worker on vacation from a full-time job
A retiree who is not looking for work
test.why: The labor force is the employed plus people actively looking. A retiree who is not looking is in neither group.

test.q: A newly certified teacher spends the summer looking for a first job. This is:
test.why: Time spent searching for a job while entering the workforce is frictional unemployment.

test.q: Actual unemployment is 8% and the natural rate is 5%. Cyclical unemployment is about:
A mayor says local nominal GDP rose 5% last year, so every family is better off. What is the best reply?
choices: GDP rises only when prices fall
Check real growth after inflation and median income, since GDP ignores who gets the gains
test.why: Nominal growth may be mostly price increases, and GDP says nothing about distribution. Real GDP and median income answer the question better.

write.prompt: A candidate for mayor says your city is booming: nominal GDP rose 6% last year and unemployment fell from 5.5% to 4.8%. Prices rose 4%, and the labor force participation rate fell from 64% to 62%. Use this unit's measures to decide whether the city really boomed. Show the numbers, and say what else you would want to know.
tips: Turn nominal growth into real growth: about 6% minus 4%.
Ask why unemployment fell: did people find jobs, or did they stop looking?
Name one thing GDP leaves out that matters to the city's families.
Take a clear position, then name the strongest point against it.
